sentences.text: This dinosaur is estimated to have reached a length of 7.5 meters and a weight between 756 and 1500 kilograms based on a single partial individual.
While Dryptosaurus was once thought to have three fingers, recent studies suggest it likely had only two functional digits, each ending in a talon-like claw measuring eight inches in length.
It possessed a lithe build and an elongated foot similar to earlier tyrannosauroids like Moros and Suskityrannus.

Fossils were discovered by fertilizer miners in New Jersey within the New Egypt Formation, where workers from the West Jersey Marl Company uncovered a theropod skeleton near Barnsboro in the summer of 1866.

On August 21, 1866, Edward Drinker Cope formally named the specimen Laelaps aquilunguis before presenting it to the American Philosophical Society, but in 1877 Othniel Charles Marsh renamed the genus Dryptosaurus because the original name Laelaps was already used for a mite.

Unlike larger tyrannosaurs such as Tyrannosaurus and Tarbosaurus, Dryptosaurus had large forelimbs with big claws and slender hindlimbs, and it possessed ziphodont dentition, characterized by sharp, blade-like, laterally compressed teeth.
It likely preyed on hadrosaurids, ornithomimosaurs, and ankylosaurs.

The species Dryptosaurus aquilunguis was originally described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1866 under the name Laelaps aquilunguis, and it is now classified as a member of the clade Eutyrannosauria, which includes Tyrannosauridae and genera like Nanotyrannus and Bistahieversor.

Othniel Charles Marsh established the family Dryptosauridae in 1890 to classify large theropods including Dryptosaurus, and Charles W. Gilmore was the first to suggest in 1946 that Dryptosaurus was related to Late Cretaceous tyrannosaurids like Albertosaurus and Tyrannosaurus.
Dryptosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 67 million years ago in the Maastrichtian stage, in what is now North America.
Some studies suggest Dryptosaurus may belong to its own family, Dryptosauridae, or to the family Nanotyrannidae.

David Chure argued in 2001 that fossil AMNH 5780 likely belongs to Allosaurus rather than Laelaps trihedrodon; Chase Brownstein argued in 2017 that Teihivenator macropus is a chimera and a nomen dubium; and it is debated whether Laelaps falculus represents a distinct species, with some suggesting it is based on juvenile tyrannosaur teeth.
